thread.title: Inspiration, insight and community draw the curious to The Edge Magazine
thread.title_full: Inspiration, insight and community draw the curious to The Edge Magazine

author: Robin Silverman
title: Inspiration, insight and community draw the curious to The Edge Magazine
text:
Imagine receiving an invitation that said, “You are invited to reconnect with yourself, with others, and with something greater.”
Would you be intrigued?
For over 34 years, readers of The Edge Magazine and attendees of its events have proven they are. What founding publisher Gary Beckman began as a simple newsprint publication has grown into a media platform with articles, podcast interviews, classes, retreats and a directory of practitioners focused on holistic living, higher consciousness and spiritual exploration.
“I believe people are being called right now to trust themselves in a deeper way,” says current publisher and Eden Prairie resident Kelly Wagner. “Through The Edge Magazine and my own work as an intuitive, I help people understand their ‘why.’ When you understand that, everything else starts to align. From that place, life becomes a lot more intentional, and a lot more magical.”
Articles and events expand awareness
Kelly says the original The Edge Magazine was “very fringe. It was really ‘woo-woo.’ But it was unique.”
Topics featured by The Edge weren’t like those found in other magazines. Metaphysics, intuition, meditation and yoga were new to most people when the magazine first published. The same was true of holistic health, conscious consumerism and energy healing. Spiritual growth and awakening or enlightenment experiences were not part of the mainstream.
To support the free publication, Beckman created paid events featuring some of the biggest names in the holistic, psychic and spiritual communities at the time.
Beckman’s Edge Life Expo included people like Dolores Cannon, a world-renowned past-life regressionist and hypnotherapist. Energy healers, holistic health experts and psychics were also featured, with the goal of helping attendees experience new modalities for healing “mind, body and soul.”
Attendees at these events could select from many different experiences. In group galleries, psychic mediums brought through messages from the deceased. Services like aura photography revealed the colored light emitted by the personal energy field surrounding an individual’s physical body.
Those seeking to deepen their meditation could take a “sound bath” created by experts playing crystal sound bowls.
Vendors at the expos sold products like herbal tinctures, local raw honey and essential oils. Jewelry, spiritual art and rare crystals were also sold.
The expos gathered a large following, which prompted Beckman to expand beyond Minneapolis and host events in St. Cloud, Des Moines, Iowa, and Fargo, North Dakota.
“People loved the publication, and they were passionate about the events,” Kelly says.
New publishers brought unique skill sets
When Beckman was ready to transition from the business, longtime employees and contributors Cathy Jacobsen and Tim Miejan took over operations in January 2009.
Eleven years later, in 2020, Kelly Wagner and her husband, Steve, heard The Edge was for sale. At the time, Kelly was a vice president of marketing in the aseptic sampling industry and was ready for a change. Steve was an award-winning graphic designer.
Between Kelly’s marketing and Steve’s graphic design skills, “I felt like we could do this,” she says.
Both Kelly and Steve were drawn to the business’s commitment to help readers and event participants grow, connect and be inspired.
“We wanted it to be more than a free newsprint magazine,” Kelly explains. “We wanted to normalize the conversation about the ‘unseen.’”
The timing of the business purchase, though, was questionable. “My husband and I moved and bought a company during COVID,” she says with a laugh.
Kelly’s optimism is fueled by her parents’ example as entrepreneurs. Her connection to the local area comes from being raised in Eden Prairie, where her children now attend school.
She is a chameleon at The Edge, serving in numerous capacities. Besides directing the marketing for the business, she also provides consulting services in marketing, sales and business-building opportunities, often for the practitioners listed in the site’s directory.
In addition, Kelly is a practicing intuitive through her business, “You’ve Got Kelly.” Her directory listing on The Edge website notes that she has the ability to “dial in” to help clients find their truth and “illuminate their path forward.”
“I can do telepathy, remote viewing, psychic mediumship — all those little fun things in my Mary Poppins carpet bag,” she notes.
She also provides business advice. “A lot of people in this space just want to be practitioners,” she says. “They don’t want to be business people. I’ve managed million-dollar trade show booths, so I am often asked to consult.”
Kelly also hosts a podcast, “The Being Curious Show.” She recently hosted her 150th episode.
Magazine themes seem timely
Currently, The Edge Magazine is a bimonthly publication. It publishes 20,000 copies six times a year.
It is available in 28 states, as well as Maui and Washington, D.C. Its print edition has its largest distribution in the Midwest, where copies are available at 450 pickup locations. The digital edition, available at edgemagazine.net, includes the same content as the print edition.
Each issue focuses on a theme. The current April/May issue looks into ancestral, elemental and earth wisdom.
Upcoming issues include: “Creativity and the Return to Wonder” in June/July; “Return of the Divine Feminine Balanced with the Sacred Masculine,” focusing on balance and harmony, scheduled for August/September; “Spiritual Harvest and Prosperity” in October/November; and “The Role of Gratitude and Positivity” in the December/January issue.
Kelly says the team works with an astrologer to help choose both the topics for issues and the timing.
“We pick our topics a year in advance,” she says. “Interestingly, it tends to be very timely when it does come out.”
The printed magazines are in high demand at drop spots listed on the website. “We get calls if it’s not at a drop spot,” Kelly says.
Readers can get a yearly subscription for $33.33.
“We’re not making money on the subscriptions, but they do help support our small business,” Kelly notes, recognizing that some people prefer to take a break from their screens or simply don’t want to be disappointed by finding their favorite drop spot empty.
EP publishers continue The Edge’s events
Under the leadership of Kelly and Steve Wagner, The Edge continues to produce events.
“If you’re curious about all these modalities, we bring in trusted vendors, all under one roof,” Kelly explains.
She says more than 1,100 people attended last year’s Psychic & Holistic Expo in Maple Grove. This year’s expo is scheduled for July 25 at the Maple Grove Community Center.
Art on the Edge attracts more than 2,000 people. It started in an art gallery in Linden Hills. Now in its fifth year, the 2026 location is set for Father Hennepin Bluff Park near the Stone Arch Bridge in Minneapolis. This outdoor event on Sept. 19 features artisans and jewels, holistic healers and readers, music and food trucks.
For those seeking a deeper or more personalized experience, The Edge also offers retreats.
“We’re creating community,” Kelly notes. “People are looking for it.”
Upcoming retreats include one in Sedona, Arizona, in November featuring Nina Roberts Salveson, the founder of Enso Yoga. An Aloha Heart Retreat in Hawaii is scheduled for February 2027. Kelly says that both retreats are already half sold out.
‘Helping people reconnect — with themselves, each other and something greater’
The Edge website calls itself “A community for higher consciousness.”
“The website is ‘choose your own adventure,’” Kelly says. Visitors find it packed with articles, listings and links that they can explore to learn more about holistic living, higher consciousness and spiritual expansion.
For those seeking practitioners of metaphysical arts, the website offers a directory of teachers experienced in a variety of modalities relating to mind, body, spirit, wellness and higher consciousness.
The Edge does not endorse any particular practitioner or practice. All listings on the website are paid. Kelly says that readers call her frequently for referrals, which she will provide from her own point of view, and only if she has had a personal experience with the practitioner.
The website also includes listings of events, classes and podcasts on topics including somatic guided imagery, shamanic journeying, creating sacred space, tarot forecasts and others.
“The Edge opens a lot of doors for me, and positions me in the community as a thought leader in this space,” Kelly says. “I’m hoping we can continue to grow by attracting people who might want to volunteer to do some of the day-to-day work.”
Those interested in volunteering or interning should contact Kelly Wagner via the website.
“At its core, Edge Magazine is about helping people reconnect — with themselves, with each other, and with something greater,” Kelly says. “Whether someone picks up the magazine, attends an event, or sits down with me for a private session, my intention is always the same: to help them feel seen, supported, and a little more aligned with the life they’re meant to live.”
